title: 2 Chronicles 32:24–33
context: Chronicles briefly notes that Hezekiah became terminally ill, prayed, and received a sign, an episode told more fully in 2 Kings 20:1–11 and Isaiah 38. It adds that Hezekiah did not respond fittingly to the benefit he received, because his heart was lifted up, bringing wrath on him and on Judah and Jerusalem, but that he humbled himself so that the wrath did not come in his days. The chapter describes his great wealth, storehouses, and the work of bringing the waters of Gihon down to the west side of David’s city, and it says that in the matter of the Babylonian envoys God left him to test him, that he might know all that was in his heart (compare 2 Kings 20:12–19; Isaiah 39). The closing notice points to the vision of Isaiah and the book of the kings of Judah and Israel for the rest of his acts. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about the danger of pride after blessing, the mercy shown to those who humble themselves, and God’s testing of the heart.

verses.text: In those days Hezekiah was terminally ill, and he prayed to the LORD; and he spoke to him, and gave him a sign.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah becoming terminally ill, praying, and receiving a sign from the LORD. God answers prayer in personal crisis (compare 2 Kings 20:1–11).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s response to his prayer as an act of grace, told more fully in Isaiah 38. Both traditions commonly read the brief notice as affirming that God hears and answers.

verses.text: But Hezekiah didn’t reciprocate appropriate to the benefit done for him, because his heart was lifted up. Therefore there was wrath on him, Judah, and Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah failing to respond fittingly to God’s kindness because his heart was lifted up. Blessing can lead to pride when gratitude fades.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the warning that even faithful servants can fall into pride (compare 1 Corinthians 10:12). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober caution after great deliverance.

verses.text: However, Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the LORD’s wrath didn’t come on them in the days of Hezekiah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah humbling himself, so that wrath did not come in his days. Humility opens the way to mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his humbling as the fruit of God’s grace (compare 2 Chronicles 7:14; James 4:6). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s mercy to the humble.

verses.text: Hezekiah had exceedingly great riches and honor. He provided himself with treasuries for silver, for gold, for precious stones, for spices, for shields, and for all kinds of valuable vessels;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah’s great riches and honor, with treasuries for many valuable things. Wealth is described as a gift from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the wealth as blessing that also brings temptation (compare Psalm 62:10). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a reminder to hold riches lightly.

verses.text: also storehouses for the increase of grain, new wine, and oil; and stalls for all kinds of animals, and flocks in folds.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see storehouses for grain, wine, and oil, and stalls for many animals. Prosperity reaches every area of life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the abundance as God’s provision for the kingdom. Both traditions commonly read the verse as describing blessing that calls for gratitude.

verses.text: Moreover he provided for himself cities, and possessions of flocks and herds in abundance; for God had given him abundant possessions.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah providing cities and flocks, for God had given him abundant possessions. The text credits God as the giver.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the explicit note that God gave the possessions as a guard against pride. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as gratitude for God’s generosity.

verses.text: This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon, and brought them straight down on the west side of David’s city. Hezekiah prospered in all his works.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah stopping the upper spring of Gihon and bringing its waters to the west side of David’s city. His practical works prosper.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the waterworks as wise provision, also mentioned in 2 Kings 20:20. Both traditions commonly hold the exact identification of the works with caution.

verses.text: However, concerning the ambassadors of the princes of Babylon, who sent to him to inquire of the wonder that was done in the land, God left him to test him, that he might know all that was in his heart.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God leaving Hezekiah to test him in the matter of the envoys, that he might know all that was in his heart. The test reveals the heart’s real condition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the test as God’s purposeful dealing with his servant (compare Deuteronomy 8:2; Proverbs 17:3). Readers in both traditions commonly agree that God’s testing is not temptation to sin and that the episode warns against pride.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his good deeds, behold, they are written in the vision of Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the rest of Hezekiah’s acts and good deeds written in the vision of Isaiah and the book of the kings. His legacy is remembered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the reference as pointing to other records of his reign (compare Isaiah 1:1). Both traditions commonly read the verse as honoring a faithful king.

verses.text: Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the ascent to the tombs of the sons of David. All Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem honored him at his death. Manasseh his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah buried among the tombs of David’s sons and honored by all Judah. His faithfulness is remembered with honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his burial as a sign of the respect earned by his reign. Readers in both traditions commonly note that Manasseh’s reign will take a very different course.
